frase_gancho.texto: A house of quarry stone and stained glass where Mario Moreno rested, and a pool with a mosaic by Diego Rivera.

puente_narrativo.texto: This house ends the tour of Cuernavaca: here you can stay in the garden or walk back to the center.

guion_corto.texto: This stop is optional: the house is not always open. “That’s the point,” Cantinflas used to say. Mario Moreno, Cantinflas, was one of the great comedians of Mexico, and this house in Cuernavaca was his resting refuge. He acquired it around the nineteen fifties. It is said that here he finished the script of El señor fotógrafo, from nineteen fifty-three, and that he received guests such as María Félix. It is a two-story house in the neocolonial style, with quarry stone walls, stained glass and gardens. Today it works as a house museum. It has art rooms from the nineteenth and twentieth centuries and photographs of Cantinflas with his friends. In the pool there is a Venetian glass mosaic made by Diego Rivera, who was his friend.

guion_largo.texto:
This stop is optional: the house is not always open and you never know when it opens. Mario Moreno was born in nineteen eleven and died in nineteen ninety-three. Under the name Cantinflas he became one of the most beloved actors in Mexico and the Spanish-speaking world. His way of speaking, tangled and full of twists, gave rise to a verb: cantinflear. And his most famous line, “that’s the point,” is still used.

This house is on Benito Juárez Boulevard, number one hundred two, in downtown Cuernavaca. It was one of Cantinflas’s several residences. He acquired it around the nineteen fifties and used it as a personal refuge. It is said that here he finished writing the script of El señor fotógrafo, from nineteen fifty-three. Among its visitors, María Félix and other figures from the golden age of cinema are mentioned.

Afterward the house almost fell into oblivion. It was restored while trying to preserve its original character. A press note from two thousand twenty-six describes it as a two-story property, in the Mexican neocolonial style, with quarry stone walls, stained glass and abundant gardens. The sources do not agree on when it opened as a museum: two thousand twenty-one or two thousand twenty-three. It is known as Cassa Gaia.

The detail that will most interest someone coming from seeing the art of the center is in the pool. There is a Venetian glass mosaic made by Diego Rivera, who was a close friend of Cantinflas. According to one note, it represents the tree of life of Gaia, the goddess of fertility. That same note says that the signature refers to Frida Kahlo, with a toad, because she called Rivera the toad. It is a press description, not an official record. What matters is that it is a mosaic by a famous muralist, made for a private pool.

There are also art rooms. According to the notes, there are ten rooms with works by nineteenth- and twentieth-century artists. Some are dedicated to the movement called Ruptura, which emerged in Mexico in the nineteen fifties. There are also photographs of Cantinflas with his friends, and a space dedicated to him.

If the house is open, take your time to see the pool from different angles. A mosaic under water changes with the light and with the movement of whoever looks at it. Ask too whether the tour includes the gardens.

If you find the door closed, you lose nothing of the tour: you can end at the Borda Garden. According to the press notes, admission is free. Hours change; check the Before You Go section.

A rest house tells things that a museum does not. Here you can see the preferences of someone who spent half his life making other people laugh: the light, the gardens, the water of the pool. And Rivera’s presence is a reminder that the great figures of Mexican art and cinema knew each other, visited each other and gave each other works.

Close the tour calmly. That is the idea of this tour: Cuernavaca is layers of power, faith and rest. Tlahuica, Franciscans, miners, emperors, muralists and comedians. They all fit in a few streets.

texto: Find the pool and the mosaic by Diego Rivera and notice the colors of the glass
Look at the stained glass and the quarry stone walls and think about what life would have been like here in the nineteen fifties
If there are photographs of Cantinflas, find one with his friends and try to recognize someone

texto.Style: Mexican neocolonial, two stories, quarry stone and stained glass
texto.Work by Diego Rivera: Venetian glass mosaic in the pool

texto.pregunta: Myth: Cantinflas only lived in Mexico City.
texto.respuesta: Reality: He had several homes. This one, in Cuernavaca, was his resting refuge since the nineteen fifties.
